analysis.one_liner: Lets victims sue police for constitutional violations even when the law wasn't clearly settled.
analysis.headline: Introduced in January 2026 and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, the bill has two sponsors and no hearing or vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would end qualified immunity — the court-made rule that protects government officers from damage lawsuits unless they violated a right that courts had already clearly established. Victims of police misconduct could sue federal, state, and local officers without clearing that hurdle, and for the first time could sue federal law enforcement officers under the same civil rights law that covers state and local police.
analysis.who_benefits: People who are beaten, shot, wrongly jailed, or otherwise harmed by police officers and want to recover money damages. Under current law, a case can be thrown out without a trial if no prior court decision had clearly established that the exact conduct was unconstitutional; the bill removes that escape hatch, so cases would be decided on what actually happened.

how_it_helps.text: It strips out the defenses officers currently use — good faith, a reasonable belief the conduct was lawful, and the absence of a clearly established right — from lawsuits under the federal civil rights statute (42 U.S.C. 1983).
It applies to federal, state, and local law enforcement officers, and it reaches cases already pending as well as ones filed after enactment.

It adds federal law enforcement officers to the civil rights statute, closing a gap in which people harmed by federal agents (for example, during a federal drug or immigration operation) often had no way to sue for damages at all.

analysis.who_pays: Officers and the governments that employ them bear the cost: more lawsuits, larger settlements and judgments, and higher insurance premiums. Cities and counties typically indemnify officers, so most payouts would ultimately come from local taxpayers, and the individual officer pays mainly in cases where the employer refuses to cover them.

drawbacks.text: Officers could face personal financial ruin over split-second decisions made in good faith, even where the law was genuinely unsettled at the time — the situation the qualified immunity rule was built to handle.
The bill applies retroactively to cases already in court, which changes the rules for defendants mid-litigation.
Since local governments usually pay judgments on their officers' behalf, the practical cost lands on municipal budgets and insurance rates, which are funded by local taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: people whose rights were violated would get their day in court, and officers would have a stronger financial and legal reason to avoid excessive force. The costs are also real and unevenly distributed — most of the money would come from city and county budgets, not from officers' own pockets, and defenders of the current rule argue it protects officers making honest mistakes in fast-moving situations. Whether the trade is worth it is a genuine policy judgment, but the current version of the bill never got far enough for that debate to happen.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or vote while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Markey introduced the bill on January 13, 2026, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
The bill has one cosponsor, a Senate Democrat, for a total of two sponsors and no Republican support.
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — has been taken since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement officers and the governments that employ them keep the qualified immunity shield, and victims of misconduct remain unable to sue unless they can point to a prior case with nearly identical facts. Because the bill never left committee, no one had to vote on it on the record.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to abolish qualified immunity and referred it to the Judiciary Committee.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 13, 2026; no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled since.

against.name: Police unions and law enforcement associations
against.what_they_did: Have pressed Congress to preserve qualified immunity, making it the sticking point that derailed prior police-reform bills; no union-backed effort to advance this bill has emerged.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors are Democrats, there is no Republican cosponsor, and the Republican majority that controls the Senate and its Judiciary Committee has taken no action on the bill.

industries.industry: Law enforcement officers and police unions
industries.note: The bill removes the legal shield that has let officers avoid damage judgments when no prior case clearly established the right they violated. Unions have consistently defended qualified immunity because it protects members from personal liability.

industries.industry: Municipal governments and their liability insurers
industries.note: Ending qualified immunity would mean more suits and larger payouts, raising city and county legal costs and insurance premiums. Insurers would gain new premium revenue even as their government customers pay more.

analysis.trajectory: With a Republican-controlled Senate and Judiciary Committee and only two cosponsors, the realistic path is that the bill sits in committee until this Congress ends in January 2027, as every prior qualified-immunity repeal has. It would only move if a major national incident forced police accountability onto the agenda or a future Congress with different leadership picked it up.
